name: Hugging Face
tagline: The GitHub of AI — models, datasets, and free live demos in one place.
pricing: Free to browse, try demos, and download most models. Paid options exist for hosting bigger demos.
whatItIs: A giant public hub where anyone publishes AI models, datasets, and small web apps called Spaces. If a new model is open-weight, it almost certainly appears here first, with a page, docs, and usually a demo you can click right now.
whyMatters: It removes the scariest beginner wall: you can try hundreds of models in your browser without installing anything, getting any key, or spending a cent. It's also where the local-AI ecosystem (Ollama, LM Studio) gets its models.
howToUse: Go to huggingface.co/models — you'll see thousands of models. Don't panic; don't scroll.
Filter: click the sort and pick 'Most downloads' or 'Trending' — popularity filters out the noise.
Pick one and read its 'model card' — the README of the model. Good ones tell you what it's for, its size, and its license.
Try it live: many models have a 'Spaces' demo — a mini web app where you type and get results immediately.
When ready for local use (see the Ollama guide), this is where you check which sizes and versions exist.
whenNotToUse: If you just want to chat with an AI, a chat app is a friendlier first step — come here when you want to browse, compare, or run models yourself.

name: GitHub
tagline: Where code lives — over 100 million projects, including most AI tools.
pricing: Free for public and private repos at beginner scale. Paid tiers add team features.
whatItIs: The world's shared hard drive for code. Every AI project you hear about — Ollama, n8n, this website — has a repo here: the code, its full history, an issue tracker, and usually a README that explains everything.
whyMatters: It's the closest thing tech has to a public library. Learning to search it, read a README, and 'star' things turns 'I heard about a tool' into 'I can actually run that tool'. Bonus: GitHub Actions gives free daily automation — which is how our freshness engine will run.
howToUse: Create a free account at github.com.
Search by keywords ('ollama', 'ai video') and sort by stars — stars are bookmarks from other developers.
Open a project and read the README first — it's the manual, and 90% of questions are answered there.
Press 'Star' to save tools for later (your stars become your personal toolkit).
When a tool says 'git clone ...', that's you downloading its code to run it.
whenNotToUse: You don't need it to just chat with AI — but the moment you want to run or build anything, a GitHub account pays for itself (it's free).

name: OpenRouter
tagline: One API key → hundreds of models. The beginner-friendly front door to AI APIs.
pricing: Free to create a key; you pay (or use free models) per request. Many models offer a free tier; others cost cents per request.
whatItIs: A single service that proxies almost every major model — the big closed labs and the open models — through one consistent API. One account, one key, one format; you can switch models by changing one string in your code.
whyMatters: Beginners usually drown in five different developer portals before their first API call works. OpenRouter collapses all of that into one key and one endpoint — the fastest path from 'I have a key' to 'it replied!'. It also serves our Phase 2 price feed: their public model list includes live pricing.
howToUse: Sign up at openrouter.ai and create a key (it looks like sk-or-v1-...).
Keep the key in a .env file — never paste it into shared code.
Send your first request (see our 'Your first API call' guide) to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions.
Browse openrouter.ai/models to compare models and prices before you build.
Out of credits or need free? Filter the model list to free models and practice on those.
whenNotToUse: Heavy production users sometimes go direct to a provider for lower latency or special features. For learning and building your first things — this is the door.

name: Ollama
tagline: Run AI models on your own machine with one command. Free, offline, private.
pricing: Completely free. Your 'cost' is your laptop's memory (RAM) — see the laptop checker.
whatItIs: A small app for Windows/Mac/Linux that runs open-weight models locally. One install, one command ('ollama run <model>'), and you have a private ChatGPT-style chat with no account, no internet needed after download, and no per-message cost.
whyMatters: It removes money and privacy from the list of beginner worries. Models run on YOUR machine: your notes, your files, your weird questions never leave it. It's also the best way to build an intuition for model sizes — 1B feels different from 8B on the same laptop.
howToUse: Download from ollama.com and install (yes, it's really this boring — good).
Open a terminal and run: ollama run llama3.2:3b — it downloads the model, then starts a chat.
Type your questions; type /bye to exit. That's the whole magic.
Check your RAM before trying bigger models (see the laptop checker) — 8GB runs small, 16GB runs most, 32GB runs big.
Optional: install Open WebUI to get a ChatGPT-style interface on top of Ollama.
whenNotToUse: If you need frontier-level quality (the absolute best reasoning), hosted big models still win — local models trade some quality for privacy and $0.

name: n8n
tagline: Visual automation: connect apps and AI without (much) code.
pricing: Free self-hosted with your own computer/server. Cloud has a free trial then paid tiers.
whatItIs: A drag-and-drop canvas where you wire triggers ('new email arrives') to actions ('summarize with AI', 'save to a sheet'). Think of it as plumbing for apps — and AI is now one of the pipes.
whyMatters: Most 'AI earns money / AI saves me hours' stories are really automation stories: AI does the thinking inside a pipeline someone built with a tool like this. Learning basic automation multiplies what one person can run alone.
howToUse: Try the cloud trial or self-host (n8n has a one-command local install if you're comfortable with a terminal).
Start from a template — n8n ships hundreds of ready automations you can load and poke.
Build your first flow around something real and boring: 'when I add a row, summarize it'.
Add an AI step: the 'AI' category nodes connect to any OpenRouter/OpenAI-compatible key.
Run it on a schedule or a trigger — and watch your boring task stop being your problem.
whenNotToUse: For a one-off task, just paste things into a chat window. Automation pays off when something repeats weekly or daily.

name: Google Colab
tagline: Free GPU notebooks in your browser — try AI code with zero installing.
pricing: Free tier includes time-limited GPU access. Paid tiers give faster GPUs and longer sessions.
whatItIs: A hosted Jupyter notebook: code cells in a web page, running on Google's computers — including real GPUs. Write Python, press play, results appear. Nothing installs on your machine.
whyMatters: GPUs are the expensive part of AI, and Colab lends you one for free. It's the standard place beginners run model experiments from tutorials — if a tutorial says 'open in Colab', that's the whole setup step.
howToUse: Go to colab.research.google.com and sign in with a Google account.
File → New notebook. You get empty cells: type code, press the play button.
Try: !nvidia-smi in the first cell — it shows you the GPU you borrowed.
Runtime → Change runtime type → pick a GPU when a tutorial needs one.
Save your experiments to Google Drive or GitHub when done (sessions are temporary!).
whenNotToUse: For chatting with models, a chat app or Ollama is simpler. Colab is for running and modifying code.

name: CapCut
tagline: Free, beginner-friendly video editor — the assemble step of most video and AI video workflows.
pricing: Free tier does almost everything a beginner needs; a Pro subscription adds fancy effects and assets.
whatItIs: A video editor (desktop, mobile, web) known for being the least painful way to cut clips, add auto-captions, drop in music, and export. AI video tools generate pieces; something still has to stitch the pieces together — usually this.
whyMatters: Every AI video pipeline ends in an editor. CapCut's auto-captions alone save beginners hours, and its timeline-and-clips model teaches you editing basics that transfer everywhere.
howToUse: Install from capcut.com (or use the web version).
Import your generated clips/images and drag them onto the timeline in order.
Use 'Auto captions' — one of the genuinely best free AI features anywhere.
Add background music from its library; watch the volume meter so music sits under voice.
Export at 1080p and check the file before publishing anywhere.
whenNotToUse: If you're aiming at professional color work or need precise control, DaVinci Resolve (also free) is the bigger, scarier sibling.

name: VS Code
tagline: The editor most developers use — now with AI helpers built in.
whatItIs: Microsoft's free code editor: a fast, friendly notepad for code with a huge extension library. It's where you'll open, edit, and run almost everything you build.
whyMatters: Beginners waste energy on editor debates that don't matter — the honest answer is: use VS Code. It opens any project (including this website's), runs terminals in a panel, and its AI extensions write half the boilerplate for you.
howToUse: Download from code.visualstudio.com and install.
File → Open Folder on any project (try it on this website's /site folder!).
Learn three keys: Ctrl-P (find file), Ctrl-Shift-P (any command), the built-in terminal (Ctrl-`).
Install the extensions for your stack as you need them — not before.
Turn on Auto Save from the File menu. Your future self says thanks.
whenNotToUse: For tiny one-file edits, any text editor works. The moment a project has folders, VS Code earns its keep.

name: DaVinci Resolve
tagline: Hollywood-grade video editing and color — the free version has no real catch.
pricing: The free version is genuinely full-featured (editing, color, Fairlight audio). One-time $295 for Studio adds AI magic masking and noise removal.
whatItIs: The editor used on actual films, free for everyone. Edit on the timeline, fix colors like a colorist, clean audio — plus newer AI features (magic mask, voice isolation, auto subtitles in Studio).
whyMatters: When CapCut starts feeling limiting, this is the natural next step that pros actually use — without a subscription. The cut page is simpler than it looks; the color page is what makes footage look 'expensive'.
howToUse: Download the free version from blackmagicdesign.com (it is a big install — clear 10GB+).
Start on the 'Edit' page: import clips, drag to timeline, cut with the blade tool.
Fix color later, not first — a good cut beats a graded mess.
Use the 'Cut' page for quick YouTube-style assembly; it hides the advanced stuff until you need it.
Export with the YouTube preset at 1080p60 — defaults are fine for beginners.
whenNotToUse: For phone-shot TikToks with captions, CapCut is faster. On weak laptops, expect lag — lower playback resolution to 1/2.

name: Adobe Premiere Pro
tagline: The industry-standard video editor — now with text-based and AI editing.
pricing: Subscription only (~$23/mo, or with the whole Creative Cloud). 7-day free trial.
whatItIs: The editor most professional YouTubers and agencies run. Its 2025+ versions added AI text-based editing (edit video by deleting words from a transcript), auto captions, and generative extend.
whyMatters: If you plan to work with clients or in a team, Premiere files are the shared language. Text-based editing is a genuine game changer for talking-head and interview content.
howToUse: Start with the 7-day trial to see if the workflow clicks before paying monthly.
Use text-based editing: transcribe, then edit the video by editing the transcript.
Auto captions in one pass — then fix only the words the AI got wrong.
Learn three shortcuts first: C (cut), V (select), space (play). That covers 80% of editing.
Export with YouTube 1080p presets; don't touch bitrate settings at the start.
whenNotToUse: Beginners burning $23/mo before earning anything. Free editors cover the first months of learning.

name: Filmora
tagline: Beginner-friendly editor with one-click effects and AI helpers.
pricing: Free with watermark export; ~$10-20/mo or one-time license to remove it.
whatItIs: A consumer video editor that sits between CapCut and Premiere: timeline editing, a big effects/template library, AI smart cutout, AI music generator and auto captions.
whyMatters: When you want pre-made transitions and title packs instead of building everything, Filmora's template library is the fastest path to a polished-looking video.
howToUse: Pick a template matching your platform (YouTube, Reels, TikTok) instead of a blank project.
Drop your clips into the template placeholders — timing is handled for you.
Use AI smart cutout to remove backgrounds without a green screen.
Preview with the watermark — only pay if you actually publish regularly.
Export 1080p; the free tier's watermark is small but disclose it if you publish.
whenNotToUse: If the watermark bothers you and you won't pay, CapCut's free export is clean.

name: Kdenlive
tagline: Fully free, open-source video editor — no watermark, no account, no limits.
pricing: Completely free and open source (GPL). No pro tier, no upsells, ever.
whatItIs: A community-built editor (runs on Windows, Mac, Linux) with timeline editing, effects, and auto-generated subtitles via whisper integration — with zero restrictions on the free version because there is only the free version.
whyMatters: The honest 'forever free' option: no watermarks, no feature paywalls, no account. If a school, budget, or privacy stance rules out subscriptions, this is the real deal.
howToUse: Install from kdenlive.org; the download includes everything (no separate codecs).
Learn the three-panel layout: project bin, monitor, timeline — same as every editor.
Use 'Automatic subtitle' (built-in whisper) for free captions.
Save often; enable autosave in settings on first launch.
Export with the default H.264 profile — it just works for YouTube.
whenNotToUse: The interface is more utilitarian than CapCut/Filmora; template fans will miss one-click styles.

name: Descript
tagline: Edit video and podcasts by editing the transcript — delete words, not clips.
pricing: Free tier: 1 transcription hour/month with watermark. Paid from ~$12-24/mo.
whatItIs: An AI-first editor built around the transcript: the video is the text. Delete a sentence and the video cuts with it. Adds studio sound cleanup, filler-word removal ('um', 'uh'), eye contact correction and AI voice cloning for patching mistakes.
whyMatters: For talking-head, tutorial, and podcast content it removes the hardest part of editing — nothing to learn about timelines. It's the fastest spoken-word pipeline in 2026.
howToUse: Upload your raw recording; transcription happens automatically.
Delete filler words in bulk with one click ('remove all ums').
Turn on Studio Sound — it makes phone/laptop audio sound recorded properly.
Cut sections by deleting transcript text; the video follows.
Export straight to YouTube or as an MP4 when happy.
whenNotToUse: Music videos, gaming montages, anything without speech — transcript editing loses its magic there.

name: Opus Clip
tagline: AI that turns one long video into ready-to-post shorts with captions.
pricing: Free tier: ~60 upload minutes/month with watermark. Paid from ~$15/mo.
whatItIs: Upload a podcast/long video and the AI finds the most engaging moments, reframes them vertical, adds animated captions, and scores each clip's virality potential.
whyMatters: Repurposing one video into 5+ shorts is the standard 2026 content strategy, and doing it by hand takes hours. This does the finding, cropping, and captioning in minutes.
howToUse: Paste a YouTube link or upload a file (link is faster and free-tier friendly).
Let it generate clips, then sort by the virality score — start with the top 2.
Check the auto-captions for names and jargon it misheard.
Tweak the hook text on the first 2 seconds — that's where retention is won.
Export and post natively per platform (don't cross-post with the same caption).
whenNotToUse: Content without talking (music, gameplay with no commentary) — the AI picks moments from speech.

name: VEED
tagline: Browser-based video editor — captions, cleanup and quick edits, no install.
pricing: Free tier with watermark; ~$12-25/mo removes it and unlocks AI tools.
whatItIs: An in-browser editor focused on the jobs beginners actually have: auto subtitles, text-to-video snippets, background noise removal, screen recording, and quick trims — nothing to install.
whyMatters: Chromebook/school-laptop users and quick-fix editors can't install heavy apps. VEED covers 'trim this, caption that, clean the audio' in a tab.
howToUse: Go to veed.io, upload or record straight from the browser tab.
Auto subtitles first — accuracy is strong and editing them is just typing.
Use 'Clean audio' to remove background hiss and noise in one pass.
Trim with the text/timeline view; don't overthink effects.
Export — on the free tier check where the watermark sits before publishing.
whenNotToUse: Big multi-track projects — it's a quick-edit tool, not a full timeline studio. And heavy uploads need a stable connection.
